## Discussion with the FAEST team

As with the other round 3 submission teams, the first part of the meeting was given over to the FAEST team, represented by Sebastian and Shibam. Since Sebastian is already familiar with how algorithm inclusion works in liboqs (he integrated Picnic in the past), the usual integration overview was skipped. As with QR-UOV last week, an inclusion PR is already open ([PR #2592](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2592), Norm), so the discussion focused on that.

### Overview of FAEST (Sebastian)

- **Construction.** FAEST is a signature scheme in the VOLE-in-the-head paradigm, which evolved from the MPC-in-the-head approach used in Picnic. Its main advantage is that the one-way function proven in zero knowledge can be built from standard symmetric primitives such as AES, rather than the custom, proof-friendly block cipher that Picnic required. This brings signature sizes down to the kilobyte range, far smaller than Picnic's.
- **Parameter sets.** The PR covers 12 variants, with fast and small trade-offs. Some are built directly from AES; the others use Rijndael with a 256-bit block size in Even–Mansour mode as the one-way function.
- **Implementations.** There are two implementations. The reference implementation is the one currently being integrated, and it can use liboqs's existing hash and AES implementations, which reduces integration overhead. The optimized implementation relies heavily on architecture-specific features (AVX2, NEON, etc.) and is written in C++. Sebastian asked whether OQS would be interested in integrating it once the reference implementation is done, noting it would be more work since it adds a new language as well as instruction-set handling.
- **Blockers.** From the FAEST team's side, the only real blocker for the reference implementation was AES-192 support. Rodrigo confirmed this has already been merged ([PR #2571](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2571)).

### Questions

**Why C++?** In answer to Rodrigo, Sebastian explained that the optimized implementation is heavily parameterized: all sizes for the trees, commitments, grinding trade-offs and so on are compile-time constants encoded as template parameters. It started as a C implementation but moved to C++ templates to make it easier to maintain and to explore the parameter space. A thin layer on top provides the NIST API, and it was also submitted to NIST as an additional implementation. Rodrigo noted that liboqs is pure C, so supporting C++ would be a significant engineering effort and would need further discussion.

**Name.** Bruce asked how to pronounce the name. Sebastian and Shibam said it is "feast", following the authors' food-themed naming lineage (Fish, Picnic, BBQ, Banquet, FAEST).

**Rijndael-256 implementation.** Bruce noted that FAEST is the third signature scheme in liboqs to use wide-block Rijndael, and asked whether the implementation was written from scratch or sourced from elsewhere. Sebastian said it was written from scratch, directly from the specification, so that the reference code maps clearly to the spec. It is used once in key generation for the Rijndael-based parameter sets, and once during signing to compute the witness values. It is only slow relative to what an optimized implementation could achieve, and is not a bottleneck: key generation is in the microsecond range. Shibam added that the main cost in signing is the GGM trees.

**Performance of the optimized implementation.** In answer to Michael, Sebastian said the optimized C++ implementation is a factor of 10 or more faster on supported architectures, thanks to CLMUL for the finite-field arithmetic, multi-block AES instructions, and optimizations in the GGM tree implementation. Some of this could be carried over to C, but there is a trade-off with keeping the reference implementation easy to follow and check against the specification. Shibam added that industry users implementing FAEST tend to work from the reference implementation, because the optimized one is hard to map to the specification when documenting it. Sebastian also mentioned a Rust implementation that gets close to the C++ performance, but it has not yet been updated for version 3.

### Status of the FAEST inclusion PR

Norm thanked Sebastian for his review of the PR over the weekend. Norm has not yet had time to go through the review comments in depth because of his day job; addressing them is the next step. The general approach appears acceptable.

Sebastian raised two points from his review:

- **NIST API vs detached signatures.** When he integrated Picnic, liboqs called the underlying implementation directly, whereas the current PR uses the NIST API, which returns the message and signature combined. The other interface returns a detached signature only. This should be considered when deciding which functions to use (some of his review comments may be confusing on this point, since he only noticed later that the NIST API is used in the integration).
- **Symbol namespacing.** Several constants and functions shared between object files in the reference implementation are not prefixed with `faest`. Sebastian offered to prefix them upstream to avoid name clashes if that helps. Rodrigo said the copy-from-upstream approach should handle most of this, and that the duplicated symbols currently showing up relate to Rijndael. Norm confirmed that copy-from-upstream is the approach being taken.

**YAML metadata.** Michael asked whether the YAML metadata file would live in the upstream repository, as for most other algorithms. Norm said he had started with that approach, but Sebastian's repository also contains some code generation; he suggested a middle ground in which the YAML lives upstream and the generation happens in liboqs. Sebastian agreed, as long as no generated files need to be stored upstream. Michael explained that the YAML holds basic information about the algorithm (authors, lengths, etc.), so keeping it upstream means changes are made where the algorithm is maintained.

**Support statement and security contacts.** Rodrigo explained that OQS now documents the level of support each submission team provides for its algorithm, and is working on a process for routing security issues for an algorithm directly to the responsible team. Once the FAEST PR is merged or close to it, he will contact the team to agree on a support level. Sebastian was fine with this.

Norm said he had picked up the long-dormant FAEST issue ([issue #2101](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2101)) only to help move things along, not to take over. Sebastian said the work is very much appreciated, as he had started on it himself but did not find the time, and liboqs has changed a lot since he integrated Picnic.

### Debian packaging of liboqs

With his Debian hat on, Sebastian asked whether OQS is interested in liboqs being packaged by Linux distributions; it was packaged by one Debian developer in 2021 but has since dropped out. Douglas said OQS never pushed for packaging. The project remains oriented around experimental algorithms; for standardized algorithms, distributions should look to OpenSSL, which supports them at a production level. If distributions want to offer experimental post-quantum algorithms, liboqs is there for that, but ideally packaged in a way that reflects this (e.g. in Debian testing or unstable rather than stable). Sebastian said he may try to get it back in and see whether there is still interest. Rodrigo mentioned that in the past liboqs-related packages had appeared on PyPI published by an independent person rather than by OQS.

### Constant-time analysis framework

Basil highlighted [PR #2449](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2449), the constant-time analysis framework that Pablo has been working on through several iterations. It now looks good to Basil and needs a second approval. The framework enables more extensive constant-time testing with Valgrind and MemorySanitizer while keeping the existing tests, so there is no loss of coverage. It currently adds manually-run extended tests for ML-KEM across many compiler configurations, which should help detect compiler-introduced constant-time regressions. Once it is merged, other algorithms can be added, which will require reviewing the outputs and adding allow-list entries; Basil expects that well-guided use of AI could speed up that analysis considerably.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (reviewers):** Provide a second review/approval for [PR #2449](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2449).

## OQS-OpenSSL 3 provider

**0.12.0 release ([PR #833](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/833)).** Rodrigo reviewed the release candidate this morning and it looks fine, with the comments about pinning to OpenSSL 4.0.3 (the latest 4.0 release), since later versions do not work because of the new hybrids. Michael has also reviewed and approved it. Norm is following through on the remaining release steps, including updating other places such as the demos. Rodrigo hopes to announce the release at the OpenSSL Conference next week; Norm expects it to be done in a day or so.

**Handling of standardized algorithms ([issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821)).** Many recent provider issues stem from how standardized algorithms interact with the provider. Currently, the provider supports an algorithm (e.g. ML-KEM) via liboqs only for OpenSSL versions that do not include it natively (before 3.5 for ML-KEM). Michael has proposed instead dropping support entirely for algorithms once they are supported in OpenSSL, regardless of OpenSSL version. Rodrigo has not yet fully reviewed the proposal. His main concern is that it could change support for existing users and possibly reduce use of the provider, though it also fits the provider's experimental focus. Norm will look at the proposal and give feedback offline.
